title: Generative AI for Images
description: Producing and editing images, and the prompting vocabulary that separates good results from poor ones.

lessons.title: How image generation works
lessons.description: Denoising steered by your words, and why that explains hands, text and counting.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Image generation works differently from text generation, and the difference explains most of its odd behaviour.

### The idea: learning to remove noise

Most image models are **diffusion models**. The training process is easier to understand backwards.

Take a real image. Add a little random noise. Add more. Keep going until it is pure static with nothing recognisable left.

Now train a model to undo one step of that: given a noisy image, predict what it looked like slightly less noisy. Do this across an enormous number of images.

To generate a new image, start with pure random noise and run the model repeatedly. Each pass removes a little noise. After enough passes, an image emerges -- one that was never in the training data, because the starting noise was random.

### Where the text comes in

The model is trained on images paired with text descriptions. So the denoising is **steered** by your prompt: at each step, it moves toward something matching your description.

This is why prompting works, and why it works loosely. You are not commanding; you are nudging a noise-removal process toward a region of possibility.

### What this explains

**Why the same prompt gives different images.** The starting noise is random. Different noise, different image, same prompt. Some tools let you fix the starting point -- a **seed** -- which makes results repeatable.

**Why prompts feel imprecise.** You are influencing a process, not specifying an output. "A red cup on the left" is a nudge, not an instruction, which is why spatial requests are unreliable.

**Why hands and text go wrong.** The model learned what images look like statistically. Hands vary enormously across images and have a precise structure that the statistics do not enforce. Text needs exact letterforms in sequence, which is a different kind of problem from "looks like a photograph". Both have improved a great deal and neither is solved.

**Why counting fails.** "Five birds" is a weak statistical signal. You will often get four or six.

**Why style transfers so well.** Style is exactly the kind of broad statistical property this process captures. Ask for watercolour and you will reliably get watercolour.

### The mental model to keep

**You are describing a region of possible images, and sampling one.**

Not commanding. Not specifying. Describing a region and taking a sample. Narrow the region with detail, and re-sample when you do not like what you got.

That framing predicts the behaviour well, and it explains why generating four variations and picking one is the right workflow rather than an admission of failure.

## Demonstrate

Two experiments that make the mechanism visible. Any image tool will do.

**One: the same prompt, four times.**

> A ceramic mug on a wooden table by a window, morning light

Generate it four times. Four different images, all matching. That is the random starting noise. Nothing is wrong.

**Two: find the known weaknesses.**

> A person holding up five fingers, and a shop sign behind them reading OPEN DAILY

Generate a few. Count the fingers. Read the sign. You will likely find at least one problem across a handful of attempts.

Now note how good everything *else* is -- the lighting, the materials, the composition. That contrast is the shape of the technology: excellent at the statistical properties of images, unreliable at things requiring exact structure.

## Practice

Write one prompt and generate it six times in the same tool.

Lay the six out together and write down what stayed constant and what varied. The constant things are what your prompt actually controlled. The varying things are what you left to chance.

Then add one detail to your prompt aimed at controlling something that varied, and generate six more. Did it work?

This is the fastest way to learn what a prompt does and does not control, and it takes ten minutes.

## What to remember

- Diffusion models generate by repeatedly removing noise, steered by your prompt
- Random starting noise is why the same prompt gives different images
- You describe a region of possible images and sample one; you do not command
- Hands, text and counting are weak because they need exact structure
- Style transfers reliably because it is a broad statistical property

lessons.title: Text-to-image
lessons.description: Subject, setting, style, lighting, framing -- and why adjectives of approval do nothing.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Text-to-image is the basic operation: describe something, get a picture of it.

### The shape of a prompt that works

Most good image prompts contain the same five things, in roughly this order:

**Subject.** What is in the picture. Be specific: "a ceramic coffee mug", not "a drink".

**Setting.** Where it is. "On a weathered wooden table by a rain-streaked window."

**Style.** What kind of image. Photograph, watercolour, line drawing, 3D render, oil painting, technical diagram. **This has more effect than anything else in the prompt.**

**Lighting and mood.** "Soft morning light", "harsh midday sun", "moody, low-key".

**Technical framing.** Close-up, wide shot, overhead, shallow depth of field. Covered properly in lesson 5.

Not every prompt needs all five. But when an image disappoints, the missing one is usually style or lighting.

### Specific beats elaborate

A common mistake is piling on adjectives: "beautiful, stunning, amazing, high quality, masterpiece, 8k, award-winning".

These do very little. They are not descriptions; they are approval. The model has no reliable notion of "masterpiece" that differs from what it does anyway.

What works is **concrete visual detail**:

- Weak: *"a beautiful stunning amazing cafe"*
- Strong: *"a small cafe with mismatched wooden chairs, hand-written chalkboard menu, plants on the windowsill, warm afternoon light through the glass"*

Every phrase in the second version names something you would see. That is the test: **could a person draw this from your words?**

### Say what you want, not what you do not

Negatives are unreliable. "A street with no cars" may well produce cars, because "cars" is in the prompt and nudges toward them.

Some tools have a separate **negative prompt** field, which does work properly. Use that where it exists. In the main prompt, describe the positive: "an empty pedestrianised street at dawn".

### Length

There is a practical middle. Too short gives generic results. Too long and later details get diluted, and some tools truncate.

Twenty to sixty words of concrete description is a good working range. Put the most important elements first.

### Generate several, always

Because the starting noise is random, the right workflow is: generate four, pick the best, refine, generate four more.

Treating the first image as the answer misunderstands the tool. Sampling is the point.

## Demonstrate

Watch a prompt improve through four rounds. Generate each one.

**Round 1.** *"A library."*
Generic. Could be anywhere.

**Round 2, add specificity.** *"A small neighbourhood library with wooden shelves and a reading table."*
Better. Now it is a particular kind of library.

**Round 3, add style and light.** *"A small neighbourhood library with wooden shelves and a reading table. Photograph, late afternoon sunlight through tall windows, dust in the air."*
Now it has atmosphere. The style word did more than anything else.

**Round 4, add framing and detail.** *"A small neighbourhood library with worn wooden shelves and one reading table stacked with open books. Photograph, wide shot from the doorway, late afternoon sunlight through tall windows, visible dust in the air, shallow depth of field."*

Compare round 1 and round 4. Nothing in round 4 is a compliment. Every addition names something visible.

## Practice

Pick something you would genuinely like an image of -- for a presentation, a post, a project.

Write it in one word. Generate four.

Now build it up in four rounds as above: specificity, then style, then lighting, then framing. Four images each round.

Lay all sixteen out. Write one sentence on which addition changed the most. For most people it is the style word, and the answer surprises them.

## What to remember

- Subject, setting, style, lighting, framing -- style matters most
- Concrete visual detail beats adjectives of approval
- The test: could a person draw this from your words?
- Describe the positive; negatives in the main prompt are unreliable
- Generate four and pick; the first image is a sample, not the answer

lessons.title: Image-to-image
lessons.description: Starting from your picture, and the sketch workflow that controls composition.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Image-to-image starts from a picture you supply rather than from pure noise. The model adds noise to *your* image and then denoises toward your prompt.

The practical consequence: **the output keeps something of the input**. How much is something you usually control.

### The strength setting

Most tools have a slider -- strength, denoising, or similar. It decides how much noise is added before the model starts working back.

**Low strength**: small changes. Same composition, same layout, adjusted style or details.

**High strength**: the input is barely a suggestion. Composition may survive; little else does.

**Middle**: the useful range for most work, where structure carries over and appearance changes.

Finding the right setting is trial and error. Start in the middle and move.

### What it is good for

**Style change while keeping composition.** A photograph turned into a watercolour, an illustration restyled, a rough render made to look finished.

**Working from a sketch.** Draw something badly -- boxes and stick figures -- and use it to control the layout. This is the most underrated use for anyone who cannot draw. You are supplying composition, which text prompts control poorly.

**Variations on something that nearly worked.** Feed a generated image back in at low strength to get near-misses of it.

**Cleaning up or finishing.** Taking something rough toward something usable.

**Consistency across a set.** Generating several images that belong together, by working from a common starting image.

### What it is not good for

**Precise edits.** "Change only the mug's colour" is an editing job, not image-to-image, which will alter things you wanted kept. Lesson 6 covers editing properly.

**Preserving faces or text.** Both will drift. Treat any recognisable face as likely to change.

**Guaranteeing anything survives.** Even at low strength, details move. Never assume a specific element is safe.

### The sketch workflow

Worth spelling out, because it solves a real problem.

Text prompts are unreliable about arrangement -- what is left, what is behind, how big. A sketch fixes that directly.

1. Draw the layout crudely. Rectangles and labels are enough.
2. Feed it in at medium strength with a full text prompt describing the finished look.
3. Adjust strength: too low and it looks like your sketch, too high and it ignores your layout.

You have now controlled composition through the image and appearance through the text, using each for what it is good at.

## Demonstrate

Two exercises.

**One: strength.** Take any photograph you have. Use the same prompt -- *"watercolour painting, soft edges, muted colours"* -- at low, medium and high strength.

Line up the three. Low keeps the photo's detail with a wash over it. High may have invented a different scene. Medium is usually what you wanted. Now you know what the slider does, which no explanation conveys as well.

**Two: the sketch.** Draw a crude layout on paper or in any drawing tool. A horizon line, a box for a building, a circle for the sun, a blob for a tree. Thirty seconds, badly.

Photograph or export it and feed it in at medium strength with:

> A landscape photograph at golden hour, a stone farmhouse, a single oak tree, low sun

Compare with generating the same prompt from text alone. The sketch version follows your arrangement. The text-only version puts things wherever it likes.

## Practice

Take something you need an image of where the **arrangement** matters -- a diagram-like layout, a scene with specific placement, a composition for a slide.

Try it text-only, four times. Note how much the arrangement varies.

Then sketch the layout and run image-to-image at medium strength, four times. Note the variation now.

Write one sentence on what the sketch bought you.

## What to remember

- Image-to-image starts from your picture; strength decides how much survives
- Low keeps structure and changes style; high keeps little
- The sketch workflow controls composition, which text prompts do badly
- Faces and text will drift; assume nothing specific is preserved
- For precise changes use editing, not image-to-image

lessons.title: Prompting for images
lessons.description: Description not instruction, and how to steal vocabulary from images you like.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Image prompting is a different skill from text prompting. The rules from module 4 mostly do not transfer, and knowing which do saves a lot of confusion.

### What carries over

**Specificity wins.** Same as text.

**Iterate, one change at a time.** Same as text, and even more necessary because of the randomness.

**Say what you want, not what you do not.** More true for images than for text.

### What does not carry over

**Instructions do not work.** "Make sure the logo is in the corner" is not followed. Image models respond to **description**, not command. Describe the image as if it already exists.

- Weak: *"Please put a small bird in the top left."*
- Better: *"A small bird in the top left of the frame."*

Even then, spatial placement is unreliable. Use image-to-image when arrangement matters.

**Reasoning does not work.** "Think about what would look good here" does nothing. There is no reasoning step to invoke.

**Negation is unreliable.** Covered already and worth repeating because it is the most common mistake carried over from text prompting.

**Long context does not help the same way.** Beyond a point, extra words dilute rather than add.

### The vocabulary problem

The single biggest gap for beginners is not knowing the words.

You want a particular look and cannot name it. The model responds well to precise visual vocabulary and poorly to vague gestures.

Worth learning, and covered in the next lesson: terms for **shot type** (close-up, wide, overhead), **lighting** (backlit, golden hour, soft diffused), **style** (line art, watercolour, 3D render, film photograph), and **composition** (rule of thirds, centred, negative space).

A useful trick in the meantime: **find an image you like and ask a multimodal model to describe it in prompt terms.** You get the vocabulary for what you were looking at, and you can reuse it.

### Structure that works

A reliable ordering, because earlier terms tend to carry more weight:

```
[style], [subject with detail], [setting], [lighting], [composition/framing], [colour/mood]
```

For example:

> Film photograph, a woman in a yellow raincoat waiting at a bus stop, wet city street at night, backlit by passing headlights, shot from across the road, muted blues with one warm highlight

Every phrase names something visible, and the style word leads.

### Iterating

Change **one element at a time**, regenerating several each round. Because output is random, a single image is not evidence that a change helped -- you need a few to see whether the distribution moved.

That is a real difference from text prompting, where one output usually tells you enough.

## Demonstrate

The describe-an-image trick, which is the fastest way to build vocabulary.

1. Find an image whose look you like. A photograph, an illustration, a poster.
2. Give it to a multimodal model with:

> Describe this image as an image-generation prompt. Cover style, subject, setting, lighting, composition and colour. Use precise visual vocabulary. Do not describe what it means -- describe what it looks like.

3. Read the result. You now have the words for the look you wanted.
4. Use that prompt, changing the subject to yours.

Most people learn more visual vocabulary from three rounds of this than from any list of terms, because it is attached to something they already wanted.

## Practice

Do the describe-an-image exercise three times with three very different images.

Collect the vocabulary that comes up. Build yourself a short list: five style words, five lighting words, five framing words that you now understand.

Then write one prompt using only vocabulary from your list, for something you actually need.

## What to remember

- Image models respond to description, not instruction -- describe the image as if it exists
- Negation and spatial placement are both unreliable
- The main beginner gap is vocabulary, not technique
- Ask a multimodal model to describe an image you like, in prompt terms
- Lead with style; change one element per round and generate several

lessons.title: Style, composition, lighting and camera
lessons.description: The vocabulary lesson -- the words that do most of the work.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This is the vocabulary lesson. These words do more for your results than any other technique in the module.

### Style

The highest-leverage word in any image prompt. Always include one.

**Photographic**: film photograph, digital photograph, documentary photography, studio photograph, polaroid, black and white photograph.

**Illustrative**: watercolour, oil painting, gouache, ink line drawing, charcoal sketch, woodblock print, children's book illustration, technical illustration, flat vector illustration.

**Rendered**: 3D render, clay render, isometric illustration, low-poly, product visualisation.

**Graphic**: minimalist poster, art deco poster, screen print, risograph, infographic, blueprint.

One style word changes an image more than twenty words of subject detail.

### Composition and framing

Where things sit and how much you see.

**Shot type**: extreme close-up, close-up, medium shot, wide shot, establishing shot.

**Angle**: eye level, low angle (looking up, makes subjects imposing), high angle (looking down, makes them small), overhead or top-down, dutch angle (tilted, unsettling).

**Arrangement**: centred composition, rule of thirds, symmetrical, negative space, tight crop.

**Depth**: shallow depth of field (blurred background), deep focus (everything sharp), bokeh.

### Lighting

The main driver of mood, and the thing beginners most often leave out.

**Direction**: backlit, side lighting, front lit, rim lighting, top-down.

**Quality**: soft diffused light, harsh direct light, dappled light, overcast.

**Time and colour**: golden hour, blue hour, midday sun, moonlight, candlelight, neon.

**Studio**: three-point lighting, single softbox, high key (bright, minimal shadow), low key (dark, dramatic shadow).

**High key and low key are worth learning properly.** They shift the emotional register of an image more reliably than almost any other pair of terms.

### Camera

Borrowed from photography, and it works.

**Lens**: wide angle (expansive, distorted at edges), 35mm (natural), 85mm portrait lens (flattering, compressed), macro (extreme close detail), telephoto (compressed distance).

**Film and finish**: 35mm film grain, high contrast, desaturated, muted palette, vivid saturated colour.

### Colour and mood

**Palette**: monochrome, warm palette, cool palette, muted earth tones, pastel, high contrast black and white, limited palette of two colours.

**Mood**: serene, tense, melancholy, energetic, austere, nostalgic. These work less reliably than concrete terms, but they do something, especially combined with matching lighting.

### Putting it together

Layer one term from each category:

> Film photograph, a lone cyclist on a coastal road, wide shot, low angle, golden hour backlighting, 35mm, muted warm palette

Seven decisions, each borrowed from photography and design. That is what separates a considered image from a generic one, and it is entirely learnable.

## Demonstrate

The single-variable experiment. This teaches the vocabulary faster than memorising it.

Fix everything except one category. Use this base:

> A wooden chair in an empty room

Now generate it six times, changing only the style: *watercolour*, *film photograph*, *3D clay render*, *ink line drawing*, *art deco poster*, *charcoal sketch*.

Six completely different images from one subject. Lay them out.

Then repeat with lighting fixed on one style: *golden hour*, *harsh midday sun*, *single candle*, *overcast*, *neon*, *low key dramatic*.

Twelve images, twenty minutes, and you will remember these words permanently because you have seen what each does.

## Practice

Build a personal reference sheet.

Pick one subject relevant to your own work. Generate it with six different style words, then six different lighting words, then four different shot types.

Save them in a document with the term under each image.

This is a genuinely useful artefact. You will consult it, and it means you never again have to guess which word gets the look you have in mind.

## What to remember

- Style is the single highest-leverage word; always include one
- Lighting is the main driver of mood and the most commonly omitted
- High key and low key shift emotional register more reliably than mood words
- Camera vocabulary from photography works
- Change one category at a time and generate several to learn what each word does

lessons.title: Editing an image
lessons.description: Inpainting, outpainting, and the three things that still give an edit away.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Editing is changing part of an existing image while keeping the rest. It is a different operation from image-to-image, which changes everything a bit.

### The main techniques

**Inpainting.** Mask a region and describe what should be there instead. Remove an object, replace a background, change a colour, add something.

This is the workhorse. Most real image work is inpainting rather than generation.

**Outpainting.** Extend beyond the original edges. Turn a portrait crop into a landscape one, or give yourself room for text.

**Instruction editing.** Some tools let you describe a change in plain language -- "make the sky stormy" -- and handle the masking themselves. Convenient, and less precise than masking yourself.

**Background removal and replacement.** Common enough to be a one-click feature in most tools.

**Upscaling.** Increase resolution, inventing plausible detail. Note the word: the detail is invented, not recovered. Upscaling a photograph of a document will produce confident, wrong text.

### Getting good inpainting results

**Mask generously.** Too tight and the result does not blend at the edges. Include some surrounding area.

**Describe the whole region, not just the change.** If you mask a person and want them gone, describe what should be there -- "empty pavement, continuing the wet cobblestones" -- rather than "remove the person". The model fills the region with what you describe.

**Match the existing conditions.** Mention the lighting and style of the surrounding image. An insertion lit differently from the scene reads as wrong even when the object is good.

**Work in passes.** Several small edits beat one large one. Each pass is easier to control and easier to undo.

**Generate several and pick.** Same as everywhere in this module.

### What stays difficult

**Faces.** Editing near a face tends to change it. Approach with low expectations.

**Text.** Adding or correcting text inside an image remains unreliable. For a poster, the right answer is usually to generate the image without text and add the text in a design tool, which lesson 7 covers.

**Consistent lighting on inserted objects.** The most common giveaway in a bad composite.

**Reflections and shadows.** Remove an object and its shadow often stays. Add one and it arrives without a shadow. Check for both.

### The honesty question

Editing photographs has a long history and the norms are not new. What has changed is how easy it is and how good the results are.

Reasonable positions, widely held:

- Editing your own creative work: fine, and always has been
- Retouching a product photo: normal commercial practice, within advertising rules
- Removing a person from a news photograph: not acceptable
- Altering an image presented as a record -- evidence, journalism, documentation: not acceptable
- Editing an image of a real person in a way that changes what they appear to have done: not acceptable, and in many places unlawful

The test that holds up: **would the people looking at this be surprised to learn it was edited?** If yes, either say so or do not do it.

Module 10 covers this properly.

## Demonstrate

Three edits on one photograph of your own. Use any tool with inpainting.

**One: remove something.** Find a distracting object. Mask it generously and describe the background that should be there, in detail, matching the lighting. Then look for the leftover shadow.

**Two: replace a background.** Mask around the subject, describe a new setting including its lighting. Judge whether the subject's lighting now matches the background. This is usually where it falls apart.

**Three: extend the frame.** Outpaint to a wider format. Note where the extension stops being convincing.

Three edits, fifteen minutes, and you will have met the three main failure modes directly.

## Practice

Take one real image you need for something.

Improve it in at least three passes of inpainting, one change per pass. Keep every intermediate version.

Then examine the final image specifically for: mismatched lighting, missing or leftover shadows, edges that do not blend, and anything that changed which you did not intend.

Write down what you found. Most people find at least two things they had not noticed while working.

## What to remember

- Inpainting is the workhorse; describe the whole region, not the change
- Mask generously and match the surrounding lighting and style
- Work in several small passes, generating options each time
- Faces, text, shadows and reflections remain the weak points
- Upscaling invents detail, it does not recover it
- Ask whether viewers would be surprised to learn it was edited

lessons.title: Posters and social media graphics
lessons.description: Generate the artwork, add the text elsewhere.
lessons.content:
## Learn

This is the most common real use of image generation for most people, and it has one rule that saves enormous frustration.

### The rule

**Generate the image. Add the text somewhere else.**

Text inside generated images remains unreliable. Even when it improves, you cannot reliably control the font, the exact wording, the spacing or the alignment -- and those are exactly what a poster depends on.

So: generate the artwork with no text, then place text over it in a design tool. Any of them will do, and most have free tiers.

This single workflow change is the difference between fighting the tool for an hour and finishing in ten minutes.

### The workflow

**1. Decide the message first.** What must the viewer know, and what should they do? A poster with a clear hierarchy of three things beats a beautiful one with no hierarchy.

**2. Decide the format.** Instagram square, story, A4 poster, slide, banner. Generate at roughly the right shape; extending later with outpainting is extra work.

**3. Generate the artwork, deliberately leaving space.** Describe the composition with room for text: *"...with large areas of clear sky at the top"*, *"...negative space on the left third"*.

Asking for space is the trick people miss. A beautiful full-bleed image with nowhere to put the headline is useless.

**4. Generate several. Pick one.**

**5. Add the text in a design tool.** Now you control everything that matters about it.

**6. Check it at actual size**, including small on a phone.

### Prompting for usable backgrounds

Backgrounds are a different job from pictures. You want something that supports text rather than competes with it.

Useful phrases:

- *"with large areas of negative space"*
- *"simple uncluttered composition"*
- *"soft gradient background, out of focus"*
- *"subject in the lower third, empty sky above"*
- *"muted colours, low contrast"* -- text sits better on this

A common mistake is generating something too interesting. A background that is busy and vivid makes the text unreadable and the poster worse.

### Consistency across a set

For several posts that should look related:

- Use the **same style vocabulary** across all of them: same style word, same lighting, same palette
- Use **image-to-image** from one another at low strength
- Fix the **seed** if your tool allows it
- Keep the same **layout, fonts and colours** in the design tool -- this does more for coherence than the images do

Consistency mostly comes from the design layer, not the generation layer. People try to solve it in the prompt and struggle.

### What to be careful about

**Brands, logos and trademarks.** Do not generate someone else's logo or a lookalike.

**Real people.** Do not generate identifiable people, especially in ways implying endorsement.

**Copyrighted characters.** Do not generate them for anything public.

**Terms of use.** Every tool has rules about commercial use, and they vary. Check before using an image for anything that makes money.

**Disclosure.** Some platforms and organisations require you to label AI-generated imagery. Check.

## Demonstrate

Make one real poster, start to finish, in about twenty minutes.

Pick something genuine: an event, a society meeting, a product, a talk.

1. Write the three things it must communicate, in priority order
2. Choose the format
3. Prompt for artwork **with deliberate empty space**, for example: *"Flat vector illustration, a group of students studying around a table, minimal style, muted teal and cream palette, large empty area across the top third"*
4. Generate six. Pick the one with the most usable space.
5. Take it into a design tool. Add your three pieces of text with clear hierarchy -- one big, one medium, one small.
6. Look at it on a phone

Notice that steps 5 and 6 are where it became a poster. Step 3 only made a picture.

## Practice

Make a set of three related graphics for the same thing -- for instance a square post, a story, and a printable A4.

Use the same style vocabulary across all three, and the same fonts and colours in the design tool.

Then show the set to someone and ask whether they look like they belong together. If not, the fix is almost always in the design layer, not the images.

## What to remember

- Generate the artwork without text, then add text in a design tool
- Prompt for negative space deliberately, or you will have nowhere for the headline
- Decide the message and hierarchy before generating anything
- Consistency comes mostly from fonts, colours and layout, not from prompts
- Check the tool's commercial terms, and avoid logos, real people and known characters

lessons.title: The image tools
lessons.description: Assistants, design tools, Adobe and dedicated generators -- what each is for.
lessons.content:
## Learn

> These tools change constantly -- features, limits and tiers all move. This lesson covers what each is **for**, which is stable. Check current capabilities yourself.

### Image generation inside general assistants

Most general assistants now generate images in conversation. ChatGPT and Gemini both do.

**Good for:** convenience, and iterating in plain language. You can say "the same but at night" and it understands the context from the conversation. For someone who does not want to learn a separate tool, this is the lowest-friction option and it is usually good enough.

**Weaker for:** fine control. Fewer knobs -- seeds, strength, precise masking -- than a dedicated tool.

### Design tools with AI attached

Canva and similar products combine generation with what you actually need afterwards: templates, fonts, layout, brand colours, export at the right sizes.

**Good for:** the whole job. This is the practical answer for posters, social posts and presentations, precisely because of lesson 7's rule. Generation and the design layer in one place.

**Weaker for:** image quality at the top end, and fine-grained control.

### Adobe Firefly and the Adobe tools

Adobe's generative features, integrated across their applications.

**Good for:** people already working in Adobe tools; editing workflows; and the licensing question -- Adobe has emphasised training on licensed and public-domain material, which matters to organisations that need to be careful about provenance.

**Weaker for:** it assumes you are in the Adobe ecosystem.

### Dedicated generation tools

Products built only for image generation, plus open-weights models you can run yourself.

**Good for:** control. Seeds, strength, precise inpainting, fine-grained settings, and with open-weights models the ability to run locally with no data leaving your machine.

**Weaker for:** friendliness. Steeper learning curve, and running locally needs capable hardware.

### Choosing

Honestly, for most people in this course:

**Start with whatever is in your general assistant.** It is already there and it is good enough to learn everything in this module.

**Add a design tool** the moment you need to put text on anything. Which is immediately, for real work.

**Add a dedicated tool** only if you hit a specific wall: you need repeatable results, precise masking, or local generation for privacy.

That progression matches actual need. Starting with a dedicated tool means learning a lot of controls before knowing which you need.

### The questions to ask about any tool

1. **What are the commercial terms?** Can you use output for something that makes money?
2. **What happens to your uploads?** Especially for images of real people or internal material.
3. **Is there an indemnity?** Some providers offer legal cover for commercial use; this matters to organisations.
4. **Can you control seeds and strength?** Decides whether you can reproduce a result.
5. **What does it refuse?** All of them refuse things; the boundaries differ.

## Demonstrate

Run the same brief through two categories and compare the experience, not just the output.

Take a real need -- a graphic for something you are doing.

**In a general assistant:** describe it, iterate conversationally three times.

**In a design tool:** generate something similar, then actually finish it -- add text, set the format, export it.

Time both. Note where each became frustrating.

Most people find the assistant faster to a good *image* and the design tool faster to a finished *thing*. That distinction is the lesson.

## Practice

Answer the five questions above for the tools you have access to. The answers are in the terms of service and the help pages.

Write them down in a short table.

Do this once, properly, and you will not have to wonder later whether you were allowed to use an image for something.

## What to remember

- Assistants are convenient and conversational; design tools finish the job
- Adobe suits people already in Adobe tools and organisations concerned with provenance
- Dedicated and open-weights tools give control, including local generation
- Start with what you have, add a design tool immediately, add a dedicated tool only on a specific need
- Check commercial terms, upload handling and indemnity before using output commercially

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 7.

:::quiz
Q. Why does the same image prompt produce different images each time?
- The model updates between requests
+ Generation starts from random noise, and different starting noise gives a different image
- The prompt is interpreted differently each time
- Image models are not deterministic by design of the training process
= Diffusion models start from random noise and denoise toward your description. Fixing the seed, where a tool allows it, makes results repeatable.

Q. Why are hands, text and counting the classic weak points?
- They were underrepresented in training data
+ They require exact structure, which a statistical process does not enforce
- They are deliberately restricted by the tool
- They only fail at low resolution
= The model learned what images look like statistically. Style is a broad statistical property and transfers reliably. Five fingers, correct letterforms and exact counts need precise structure that the statistics do not guarantee.

Q. Which addition typically changes a generated image most?
- Adding "high quality, 8k, masterpiece"
+ Adding a style word such as "watercolour" or "film photograph"
- Adding more adjectives about the subject
- Making the prompt longer
= Style is the highest-leverage word in any image prompt. Adjectives of approval do very little; the model has no reliable notion of "masterpiece" separate from what it does anyway.

Q. What is the test for whether your image prompt is specific enough?
- Is it over thirty words?
+ Could a person draw this from your words?
- Does it include a style and a lighting term?
- Does it avoid all negatives?
= Every phrase should name something visible. "Beautiful stunning cafe" fails the test; "mismatched wooden chairs, chalkboard menu, plants on the windowsill, warm afternoon light" passes it.

Q. You need a specific arrangement -- this on the left, that behind it. What works best?
- A longer, more precise text prompt
- Repeating the spatial instruction twice
+ Sketching the layout crudely and using image-to-image
- Using a negative prompt for the wrong arrangement
= Text prompts control arrangement poorly because you are nudging a process rather than commanding it. A sketch supplies composition directly, and the text prompt then controls appearance. Each is used for what it is good at.

Q. When inpainting to remove an object, what should the prompt describe?
- The object to be removed
+ What should be in that region instead, matching the surrounding lighting and style
- Both the object and its replacement
- Nothing -- the mask is enough
= The model fills the masked region with what you describe. "Remove the person" is an instruction; "empty pavement continuing the wet cobblestones, same overcast light" is a description of the region. Then check for the leftover shadow.

Q. What is the rule for making a poster?
- Generate the image with the text included, then correct the text by inpainting
+ Generate the artwork with no text, then add text in a design tool
- Use a tool that specialises in text rendering
- Generate text and image separately and ask the model to combine them
= Text inside generated images is unreliable, and even when legible you cannot control font, spacing and alignment -- which is what a poster depends on. This one workflow change saves more frustration than any other in the module.

Q. What should you prompt for when generating a poster background?
- The most visually striking image possible
+ Deliberate negative space, and a composition that supports text rather than competing with it
- Maximum colour saturation for impact
- A tightly cropped subject filling the frame
= A beautiful full-bleed image with nowhere to put the headline is useless. Asking for "large areas of negative space" or "subject in the lower third, empty sky above" is the step people miss.

Q. Where does visual consistency across a set of graphics mostly come from?
- Using the same prompt for all of them
- Using the same model version
+ The design layer: same fonts, colours and layout
- Generating them all in one session
= People try to solve consistency in the prompt and struggle. Shared style vocabulary and a fixed seed help, but fonts, colours and layout do most of the work.

Q. What does upscaling an image actually do?
- Recovers detail that was lost in compression
+ Invents plausible detail at higher resolution
- Increases file size without changing the image
- Sharpens existing edges only
= The detail is generated, not recovered. This matters most for anything with text or precise values: upscaling a photograph of a document produces confident, wrong text.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 8. If you missed questions, the fix for this module is doing the single-variable experiments from lesson 5 rather than rereading -- the vocabulary sticks when you have seen what each word does.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: a poster from brief to final
lessons.description: One real brief, start to finish, tested on an actual person.
lessons.content:
Forty-five minutes. You will take a real brief from nothing to a finished poster you would actually use.

## Before you start

You need an image generation tool and a design tool. A general assistant that generates images plus any free design tool is enough.

Pick a **real** brief. Something you actually need or could plausibly use: a society event, a talk, a small business promotion, a community notice, a study group.

## Step 1: The brief, in writing

Before generating anything, write down:

- **Who** it is for -- the actual audience
- **The three things** it must communicate, in priority order
- **The one action** you want the viewer to take
- **The format** -- exact dimensions or at least the shape
- **Where it will be seen** -- phone screen, noticeboard, printed A4

Five answers. This takes five minutes and it determines everything after.

## Step 2: Decide the look

Using module 7's vocabulary, decide three things before you prompt:

- A **style** word
- A **lighting** term
- A **palette**

Write them down. Committing before you generate stops you drifting through whatever the tool happens to produce.

## Step 3: Prompt for artwork with space

Write your prompt using the structure from lesson 4: style first, then subject, setting, lighting, framing, colour.

Include an explicit instruction for negative space where your text will go.

> [style], [subject with concrete detail], [setting], [lighting], [framing], [palette], large areas of negative space across the [top / left third / bottom]

Generate **at least six**. Do not settle for the first.

## Step 4: Pick, and say why

Choose one. Write one sentence on why it beat the others -- usually it is the one with usable space and the least competing detail, not the prettiest.

:::hint Everything I generated is too busy for text
That is the most common result. Add "simple uncluttered composition", "soft out-of-focus background", "muted low contrast colours" and reduce the subject detail. You are making a background, not a picture; a background that is interesting in its own right is usually the wrong background.
:::

## Step 5: Refine it

At least two passes of editing or regeneration, one change each:

- Inpaint out anything distracting
- Outpaint if you need a different aspect ratio
- Adjust the prompt and regenerate if the composition is nearly right

Keep every version.

## Step 6: Add the text

In the design tool. Three pieces of text with clear hierarchy: one dominant, one supporting, one small.

Make deliberate decisions about font, size, colour and position. Note them down -- you will reuse them if you make a set.

## Step 7: Test it

Three checks:

1. **On a phone.** Is the main message readable at that size?
2. **At a glance.** Look away, look back for two seconds. What did you take in? Was it the thing you wanted?
3. **On someone else.** Show it to one person and ask what it is for and what they should do. Do not explain first.

Record what the third check revealed. It almost always reveals something.

## Step 8: Write it up

1. Your brief, all five answers
2. Your three look decisions
3. Your final prompt, and how many images you generated
4. Why you chose the one you did
5. Your two refinement passes
6. Your text hierarchy decisions
7. What the three tests revealed, especially the person
8. What you would do differently

Include the first image you generated and the final poster, side by side.

## What good looks like

A strong submission shows the poster **working**, not just existing. The person test is the evidence -- if someone looked at it for two seconds and correctly said what it was for, it works.

A strong submission also reports the person test honestly when it went badly. "She thought it was about a concert" is a more useful finding than "she liked it", and it is what the step is for.

lessons.title: Assignment: a visual identity for a small project
lessons.description: Four coherent graphics plus the rules behind them, marked against a rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Create a **visual identity** for a small real project: a coherent set of graphics that clearly belong together, plus the documented rules that make them consistent.

One poster is a picture. A set that holds together is a design system, and that is a genuinely different skill.

## Choose a real project

A society, an event series, a small business, a podcast, a newsletter, a study group, a personal portfolio.

Real is better. If you must invent one, give it a specific audience, a specific purpose and a specific tone.

## What to submit

One document, **900 to 1300 words**, plus the images.

### 1. The project and its audience

What it is, who it is for, and the tone it should project -- three adjectives, each with a reason. "Professional" means nothing on its own; "approachable, because our members are first-years who find the society intimidating" means something.

### 2. The visual rules

Your system, stated so someone else could follow it:

- **Style**: the exact style vocabulary you use in every prompt
- **Palette**: your colours, with hex codes
- **Typefaces**: heading and body, with sizes or relative scale
- **Composition**: where text sits, how much negative space, any recurring layout
- **What is never done**: at least two rules about what breaks the identity

The last one matters. A system without prohibitions is not a system.

### 3. The set

**At least four** finished graphics with different jobs and formats. For example: a square social post, a story format, a printable A4, and a slide or banner.

They must be recognisably the same identity while doing different jobs. Four crops of one image is not a set.

### 4. The process

For **one** of the four, show the full working:

- The brief
- Your prompt, final version
- At least four generated candidates, shown
- Which you chose and why
- Every editing pass
- The finished graphic

This section is where you demonstrate the technique from the module rather than just the outcome.

### 5. The consistency test

Show the four together. Then answer honestly:

- What actually makes them cohere? Be specific -- is it the palette, the typeface, the composition, the style?
- Where does the consistency break down?
- Show the **rejected** attempt that did not fit, and say why.

The rejected attempt is required. Everyone has one, and showing it demonstrates you were judging against a system rather than accepting what came out.

### 6. Rights and honesty

Short, specific, and marked:

- Which tools you used, and what their commercial terms allow
- Confirmation that you generated no logos, identifiable real people or known characters
- Whether this project would need to disclose AI-generated imagery, and to whom
- Any image where a viewer would be misled about what it depicts

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Project and tone, 10 marks.** Full marks for a real project with three tone adjectives, each justified by something about the audience. Marks lost for generic adjectives with no reason.

**Visual rules, 20 marks.** Full marks for a system specific enough that another person could produce a fifth graphic that fits -- named style vocabulary, hex codes, typefaces, composition rules, and at least two prohibitions. Marks lost heavily for missing prohibitions.

**The set, 25 marks.** Full marks for four finished graphics with genuinely different jobs and formats that clearly cohere. Marks lost for four variations of one thing, and for graphics that are unfinished -- no text, wrong format, not exported properly.

**The process, 20 marks.** Full marks for one graphic shown end to end: brief, prompt, four or more candidates, selection reasoning, editing passes, result. Marks lost where only the final image is shown, which demonstrates nothing about method.

**Consistency test, 15 marks.** Full marks for a specific analysis of what creates the coherence, an honest account of where it breaks, and a shown rejected attempt. Marks lost for "they all look similar" with no analysis, and for no rejected attempt.

**Rights and honesty, 10 marks.** Full marks for all four points addressed specifically. Marks lost for a generic statement that no rules were broken.

## What will cost you marks

**A set that is four crops of one image.** Different jobs and different formats, or it is not a set.

**Visual rules too vague to follow.** The test is whether another person could make a fifth graphic that fits. "Modern and clean" fails that test.

**Only showing finished work.** The process section is a fifth of the marks and it needs the candidates you rejected.

**Text generated inside images.** Lesson 7 exists for a reason. Text belongs in the design layer, and generated text in a submitted graphic suggests the workflow was not followed.

**No prohibitions and no rejected attempt.** Both signal that nothing was actually being judged against.

:::hint My four graphics look related but I cannot say why
Put them side by side and remove one variable at a time in your head. Would they still cohere with different colours? With a different typeface? With a different style word? The one whose removal breaks it is doing the work. Usually it is the palette and the typeface -- which is worth knowing, because it means your consistency lives in the design layer and your prompts matter less than you thought.
:::
